rv.q: Meticulously off-handed, it’s funny and sad, a performance to be savored in a totally engaging little triumph of a show.

Mark Rylance is once again ruling audiences at the Belasco Theater, where the strangely enchanting “Farinelli and the King,” Claire van Kampen’s shimmering fairy tale for grown-ups, opened on Sunday night.
While it would be satisfying enough to simply embrace Rylance's mastery and the glorious works of (mostly) Handel, there is a more significant message
Like you do if you are Rylance, who dives deep inside wacky Philippe in a performance as empathetic as it is seemingly spontaneous.
Watching Rylance convey the pain, fear and vulnerability of that striving is heart-rending and unforgettable.

Unlike in Alan Bennett’s play The Madness of George III, and its film adaptation, the deteriorating mental health of a monarch here doesn’t constitute a sustaining narrative arc, even if Rylance’s commanding performance remains the center of attention.
The result is a show that is all frosting and no cake.
The pleasures of John Dove's production—the music, Rylance's halting propulsion, Jonathan Fensom's sumptuous sets and costumes—gleam to no purpose, real jewels glued to a trinket crown.
But mad kings could easily become a specialty with this actor, who sees the pathos and the ridiculousness of the royal personage, and warmly embraces them both.
But the truth is that Davies doesn’t really sound anything like Farinelli — or even the way he’s described in the play.

The last scene of Farinelli and the King is achingly beautiful, one of those rare theater experiences in which you feel yourself to be in the presence of so much truth and beauty that you want to see it all over again.
Mark Rylance is unparalleled as an actor.

The juxtaposition of king and singer, along with Jonathan Fensom's design elements and the Baroque musical performances by the skilled musicians under Robert Howarth's direction, makes for a lively and lovely theatrical experience.
Thankfully, there's Mark Rylance — theatre royalty, and once again we bow to his God-given gifts.
Rylance, who excels at playing sad and strange characters, gives a full-bodied and endearing performance that combines volatile behavior and over-the-top comedy with gentle contemplation.
Whatever, your eyes and ears will leave Farinelli happy indeed.
After the king exits for good, only the superb music can keep the audience awake.
With this cast led by Mark Rylance, Farinelli and the King is a polished and stylish entertainment with its authentic 18th century ambiance.
Dove's production is a total delight to the senses.
Fans of trained actors filling Broadway houses with the richness of their unamplified voices (not to mention those who believe electric lights are overrated) have reason to rejoice.
English playwright Claire van Kampen’s fact-based but liberally embroidered drama isn’t so sensational — and can't get past one obstacle.

With the script playing to Rylance's strengths, such as asides to the audience and jolts of anachronistic language played for laughs, the imbalance of power in the two leading roles keeps the piece from fulfilling its high potential.
While van Kampen’s quasi historical drama is enjoyable, the play ultimately leaves you unfilled.
Any time Rylance is available on stage to a New York audience, it’s impossible not to recommend you see him.
Van Kampen’s disjointed storytelling and John Dove’s pedestrian direction, however, turn it into something nearer soap opera — but without either the intrigue or the sex of that lesser genre.
His final Lascia, ch’io pianga would make stones weep.
Enchanting and funny, Farinelli and the King is a wonderful opportunity to see one of our century's finest actors in a role custom-crafted for his talents.
It was absolutely thrilling to watch the transformation that brought him down from uncontrollable rage to blissful contentment.
He’s like theatrical quicksilver and, as usual, is fascinating to watch.
Dove's marvelous staging, set among Jonathan Fensom's sumptuous set and costumes, rises to the level of his collaborators.
Rylance is the main attraction, commanding the show with his supple wit, weirdness, and edge of danger as he tries to hold onto his elusive mind.
We get a sense of the mood, invented but inspired.
And Sam Crane brings an authentic vulnerability to his role as Farinelli that counterpoints brilliantly with the tempered desperation of Mark Rylance’s Philippe.
It is a visual tour de force and scores with Mark Rylance's performance and Farinelli's glorious arias.
Faults aside, “Farinelli and the King” remains a delightful present of a show.
All the passion of this play indeed is held at last fully in his sweet counter-tenor and his stunning “Let Me Weep.”
Structurally, the plays leaves much to be desired, as it’s unsure of what it wants to accomplish.
Just give the Tony right now to Mark Rylance, who turns in an exquisite portrayal of a King gone mad in Claire van Kampen’s Farinelli and the King.
If Farinelli and the King gets bogged down now and then – and it does – it also has its memorable elements, including its impeccable sense of time and place.

The relationship between the two title characters of “Farinelli and the King” and a well-voiced falsetto bring out the best of the new Broadway play having a limited run at the Belasco Theatre on Broadway.

"The performances in the three major roles are almost enough to compensate for the uneven nature of the play...The always brilliant Rylance is working very hard to keep this not-quite-filled balloon afloat. The flaws in the structure make it hard, but his talents are vast, and he almost pulls it off...But the story lets him, and us, down.

But for the performance of Rylance, who is as always remarkable, and Davies, who is a delicious surprise and deserving of the two final bows that Rylance engineers, Farinelli and The King remains a tedious bit of business.
But beyond its premise of music having curative powers, which now has some empirical evidence to support it, Farinelli and the King doesn’t contribute greatly to the advance of modern playwriting.
The story itself is very compelling but, as a play, it leaves one empty and unfulfilled.

cn.t: Rylance dazzles as the mad king, earning near-universal raves, and countertenor Iestyn Davies's Handel arias are transcendent. But van Kampen's thin script divides critics, leaving many to call it a gorgeous showcase carried more by its stars than its story.

vs.sum: The Belasco Theatre offers stunning ambiance with its historic Tiffany lamps and stained-glass ceiling, but suffers from tight legroom typical of older venues. While sound quality is generally good, sightlines can be inconsistent, especially from side orchestra seats.
